candidates.title: Every AI Agent Action Needs a Receipt
candidates.author: Future AGI
candidates.reason: The reader asks a concrete architecture question about preventing an independent verifier from becoming a single point of trust.
candidates.evidence: The response distinguishes timeout ambiguity from failure, identifies double-application risk during retries, and asks how the verifier itself should be governed.
candidates.draftResponse: That is the right failure mode to challenge. I would avoid a singular verifier and use a tiered verification quorum: an authoritative system-of-record read, a policy-specific postcondition check, and an independently operated evaluator for high-impact actions. Shadow cases, canaries, and fault injection then test the verification layer itself, so trust rests on diverse evidence and visible disagreement rather than one component.

candidates.draftResponse: Agreed that preference learning will make the experience smoother, but preference is not the same as consent or delegated authority. I would measure preference accuracy together with explicit-override rate, unauthorized-action rate and recovery time.

candidates.title: Production reliability begins after the demo
candidates.author: Abhishek Bhattacharjee
candidates.reason: Fresh, source-specific production-AI discussion covering incomplete inputs, duplicate events, API timeouts, system disagreement and high-consequence actions.

I would require 10,000 replayable cases across missing fields, duplicate events, conflicting systems, timeouts and high-consequence actions, then track false-accept rate, duplicate-effect rate, p95 recovery time and the percentage of runs with reconstructable receipts. “Keeps working” should mean bounded failure and verified recovery, not merely higher uptime.

candidates.title: Securing the full execution graph of an AI agent
candidates.author: Samvad G
candidates.reason: Directly advances the account position on transitive authority, trusted execution graphs and blast-radius containment.

I would calculate effective privilege as direct grants plus reachable actions through tools, artifacts, CI/CD and trusted identities, then test maximum propagation depth, unauthorized state changes per 1,000 runs and mean time to revoke every reachable edge. Sandboxing one process cannot contain a chain whose later nodes still trust its output.

candidates.title: Goal-based agents need budgeted authorization leases
candidates.author: Manjeet Singh
candidates.reason: High-fit security discussion about persistent goal pursuit, zero trust for agents and the limits of sandboxes and monitoring.

candidates.draftResponse: The reported 13-hour compromise is a failure of goal scoping and control latency, not simply a sandbox failure. I would represent every goal as a budgeted authorization lease: permitted action classes, maximum delegation depth, time and spend caps, prohibited resources and hard expiry—then measure privilege-escalation attempts per 1,000 tool calls, containment latency and kill-switch completion p95.

candidates.title: Healthcare AI production controls and reviewer queues
candidates.author: Koushik Lahiri

For prior authorization, I would add high-impact exception recall and a reviewer-queue SLO: percentage of unsafe or ambiguous cases routed before consequence, p95 approval latency, false-accept rate and reversal time. Evidence-before-action works only if the human queue can keep pace with arrival volume.

candidates.title: The 53-point trust gap in autonomous finance
candidates.author: Victor Yaromin

candidates.draftResponse: The 71% buyer-demand figure versus 18% audit confidence creates a 53-point trust gap. The primary KPI should be the percentage of consequential actions independently reconstructable within a defined SLA.

candidates.title: Agentic AI Governance: From Task Performance to Behavioural Science
candidates.author: Ritvik Shyam
candidates.reason: Adds an action-authority dimension and a measurable longitudinal evaluation matrix to the article’s proof-of-conduct framework.
candidates.evidence: Full article reviewed in the signed-in Medium UI. Published June 5, 2026 with two visible responses; it connects long-horizon behavioral divergence, heterogeneous agents, handoff integrity and enterprise incident management. No response by Aditya Singh was visible.
candidates.draftResponse: The move from proof-of-task to proof-of-conduct is important. I would make it operational with a longitudinal evaluation matrix: behavioral drift by run horizon, downstream-error propagation across handoffs, override quality under time pressure and recovery after contradictory context. One missing dimension is authority: identical behavior becomes materially different when one agent can only recommend and another can change business state. Every conduct metric should therefore be segmented by action class and reversibility.

candidates.title: Runtime AI Governance: A Practitioner’s Playbook for Governing Agentic AI Systems

The policy gate then needs an evidence threshold and an outcome-verification receipt, measured through evidence-freshness coverage, false-allow rate, reviewer-escalation p95 and the percentage of consequential actions reconstructed end to end.

candidates.title: Benign intent can still produce an adversarial cause chain

candidates.title: Healthcare AI review-queue capacity

candidates.title: Learned skills require task-bound permission leases

candidates.title: Cyber insurance and exposure-weighted autonomy

candidates.title: Node compromise versus governing-system compromise

candidates.title: Autonomous finance with action-time authority

candidates.title: Verifier-owned receipts as a day-one requirement

I would make verifier-owned receipts a day-one requirement for any workflow that can change money, identity, customer commitments, or production state; the maturity metric is receipt coverage of high-consequence actions, not the number of logs retained.

candidates.title: Versioned outcome contracts for AI economics

candidates.title: Run-time risk scoring needs a continuously evaluated privilege graph
candidates.author: Samvad G
candidates.reason: Samvad asked a specific architecture question in response to the published account comment: dynamic run scoring versus a continuously evaluated privilege graph.

candidates.draftResponse: I would use both: the continuously evaluated privilege graph is the system of record, and the run-specific score is the authorization decision. The graph should type identities, tools, artifacts, workflows, data domains and trust assertions; each edge needs a lease, delegation depth, sensitivity, reversibility and verification state. At action time, recompute risk when an artifact hash, tool version, identity lease or upstream trust assertion changes. I would track maximum reachable privilege per run, critical paths without an independent postcondition, stale trust-edge rate and p95 time to revoke every affected path. A static graph becomes stale; a per-run score without the graph misses systemic blast radius.

candidates.title: The conversation around AI in banking has shifted.

candidates.title: AI can make one step ten times faster and leave the entire process exactly as slow as before.
